tier_reason: The README 'Current figures' table matches the record exactly, and the native-C side has every A ingredient on paper (bench/lcms_c/bench_content_matrix.c driven by bench/reproduce.js, gcc 9.3.0 in WSL2, -O2/-O3 per workflow, Ryzen 7 7700X). It stays C because the project itself says the native lcms numbers are being re-measured with corrected lcms API calls after the LittleCMS author's issue #6 and should not be quoted further, and the README figures do not match the current generated docs/BenchResults.md (jsCE 1.6.0 photo row: 112.2/113/81.2/81/110.6 MPx/s) or docs/LcmsComparison.md (jsCE 1.5.0: 119.6/121.5/82.0/81.3/118.9); the lcms-wasm baseline is a prebuilt npm package whose Emscripten flags are not stated.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Native baseline: lcms2 2.18 (MIT core, no plugins) built with gcc 9.3.0 (Ubuntu 9.3.0-17ubuntu1~20.04) under WSL2 Ubuntu 20.04, best of -O2 (RGB-source workflows) and -O3 (CMYK-source and soft-proof) after a seven-set CFLAGS sweep, pinned with taskset -c 0. jsColorEngine runs on Node v24.16.0 under Windows 10 x64 (V8 JIT, no compiler flags). lcms-wasm 1.0.5 (LittleCMS 2.16 compiled to wasm32 with Emscripten) is the prebuilt npm package; its build flags are not stated.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README 'Current figures' table (Ryzen 7 7700X, one thread, Node 24, 1 MPx photographs), int-wasm-simd MPx/s with ratios vs lcms-wasm and vs native C lcms2: RGB to Lab 120.3 (3.6x, 1.8x), RGB to CMYK 119.3 (3.4x, 1.9x), CMYK to RGB 78.6 (3.1x, 2.0x), CMYK to CMYK 80.8 (3.5x, 2.2x), RGB to RGB soft-proof 115.9 (3.4x, 2.1x), RGB to RGB matrix 117.6 (1.8x vs lcms-wasm, 0.71x vs native C). docs/LcmsComparison.md (2026-08-19, jsCE 1.5.0) gives the absolute native lcms2 figures: 65.6, 61.9, 40.0, 35.6, 56.9 and 164.5 MPx/s (matrix). The 1.5.5 fused matrix-shaper kernel reaches 328 MPx/s against 119 for jsColorEngine's own CLUT path (README); that is an internal comparison, and LcmsComparison.md says the matrix head-to-head against lcms has not been re-run.
corrections.caveats: Issue #6 (opened 2026-05-17 by mm2, the LittleCMS author, now closed) says the native benchmark used incorrect lcms API calls and that lcms plugins give 'an easy 10x improvement, sometimes more'. The README still says the native-C numbers are being re-measured with corrected API calls before they are quoted further, yet the same README shows them in its current table, so treat the vs-native-C column as provisional (the vs lcms-wasm ratios are stated to be unaffected). The README table does not match the current generated docs/BenchResults.md or docs/LcmsComparison.md exactly. Host asymmetry: the JS runs on Windows, native lcms under WSL2 on the same CPU. Different work: jsColorEngine bakes the transform into an 8-bit 33^3 or 17^4 CLUT and interpolates it with 128-bit WASM SIMD, while lcms2 (flags = 0) builds its own precalculated device link and interpolates it with scalar code; outputs agree within 1 LSB (96.8-99.2% bit-exact), not bit-identical. lcms with the GPL fast_float plugin reaches about 455 MPx/s on matrix RGB to RGB (LcmsComparison.md) and is not in the head-to-head. Single machine, first-party. Language filter mismatch: the library is JavaScript plus inline WebAssembly, not C or C++, and is usable from C++ only by embedding a JS/WASM runtime. The baseline (Little CMS) is not on the color-and-resampling list (ImageMagick, stb_image_resize), and neither of those is measured.
corrections.language: JavaScript (inline WebAssembly SIMD kernels); C appears only in bench/lcms_c, the lcms2 baseline harness

notes: Numbers match the README; the project's own docs contradict each other on whether the native-C column is final, so C stands. The language correction is outside verify.py's CORRECTABLE set; record it as a decision override if wanted.

tier_reason: All quoted timings are in readme.md (BenchmarkDotNet ShortRun tables, Xeon W-11855M and Snapdragon, .NET 6.0.10). The harness is the public third-party bleroy/core-imaging-playground (NetCore/LoadResizeSave.cs), but the MagicScaler author ran it, locally modified (constant UnrollFactor, WarmupCount=3 against upstream's 5) and with Nov 2022 package versions, while upstream master now targets net10.0, MagicScaler 0.15.0 and Magick.NET 14.15.0; the native libraries are prebuilt NuGet binaries with unstated flags. First-party run, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Load, resize to 150 px, save 12 JPEGs of about 1 MP (BenchmarkDotNet ShortRun means). Windows 10 x64, Xeon W-11855M: MagicScaler 46.85 ms vs ImageMagick (Magick.NET-Q8 12.2.0) 345.99 ms, about 7.4x (derived from page data); NetVips 100.92 ms, SkiaSharp 117.43 ms, ImageSharp 115.90 ms, System.Drawing 354.73 ms. Ubuntu 20.04 x64, same CPU: 99.8 ms vs ImageMagick 522.6 ms, about 5.2x (derived from page data); NetVips 380.5 ms, System.Drawing 271.7 ms. Windows 11 ARM64 (Snapdragon): 65.72 ms vs ImageMagick 588.63 ms, about 9.0x (derived from page data). Linux ARM64 (Raspberry Pi 4b): 214.7 ms vs ImageMagick 1,688.5 ms. Resize-only synthetic (blank 1280x853 to 150x99, Windows x64): 621.8 us vs ImageMagick 39,426.5 us, which the author says to take with a grain of salt.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: .NET 6.0.10 RyuJIT (X64 AVX2; Arm64 AdvSIMD), SDK 7.0.100-rc.2 on Windows x64 and SDK 6.0.402 on Ubuntu and Windows ARM64; BenchmarkDotNet 0.13.2.1974-nightly ShortRun (IterationCount=5, WarmupCount=3, LaunchCount=1, UnrollFactor=32 or 8). ImageMagick (Magick.NET-Q8-AnyCPU 12.2.0), libvips 8.13.2 and libjpeg-turbo (PhotoSauce.NativeCodecs.Libjpeg 2.1.4-preview1) are prebuilt NuGet binaries; their compiler flags are not stated.
corrections.hardware: Intel Xeon W-11855M 3.20 GHz (6 cores, 12 threads) on Windows 10 x64 and Ubuntu 20.04; Snapdragon Compute Platform on Windows 11 ARM64; Raspberry Pi 4b 2GB on Ubuntu 22.04 ARM64
corrections.caveats: First-party run of a locally modified copy of the public core-imaging-playground suite; results date from Nov 2022 package versions (MagicScaler 0.13.2). End-to-end JPEG decode, resize and encode with file I/O, not pure resampling, and the JPEG codec under MagicScaler is native libjpeg-turbo (C) via PhotoSauce.NativeCodecs.Libjpeg. Different work from the ImageMagick baseline: MagicScaler's default HybridMode (FavorQuality) may use the decoder or a lower-quality scaler to shrink to an intermediate size first (ratio 2 for about 1 MP to 150 px, derived from ProcessImageSettings.HybridScaleRatio), then resamples in linear light with sharpening; the Magick.NET path decodes the full image (no size hint), resizes in gamma-encoded space with ImageMagick's default filter on a Q8 build with OpenCL disabled. NetVips' Thumbnail also shrinks on load. MagicScaler's margin over ImageMagick is smaller on Linux x64 (5.2x) than on Windows x64 (7.4x), while its margin over NetVips is larger on Linux (3.8x) than on Windows (2.2x) (both derived from page data). Language filter mismatch: C#/.NET, not callable from C++. ImageMagick (on the category list) is present; stb_image_resize is not.
corrections.language: C# (.NET); native codec plugins wrap C libraries (libjpeg-turbo in the benchmark)

notes: All numbers verified in readme.md. Fixed a wrong caveat: the NetVips margin is larger on Linux x64, not smaller. The decoder-assisted hybrid scaling makes the thumbnail comparison favour MagicScaler on work done, not only on code speed.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the libvips 'Speed and memory use' wiki table, an independent and widely cited suite with public code (libvips/vips-bench pillow.py vs im.sh), measures pillow-simd 9.5.0 at 1.51 s against ImageMagick 7.1.1 convert at 4.44 s on a Threadripper PRO 3955WX, but the pillow-simd build flags and compiler are not stated, so not A. The first-party pillow-perf data (c5.large.txt, testsuite/run.py, auto/run.sh with -msse4/-mavx2) alone would be C: compiler and exact CPU model are not printed.

corrections.claimed_speedup: pillow-perf c5.large.txt, 2560x1600 RGB, single core, Pillow-SIMD 7.0.0.post3 -mavx2 vs Wand (ImageMagick 6.9): to 320x200 Lanczos 0.00523 s vs 0.10633 s, about 20x; bilinear 0.00192 s vs 0.03792 s, about 20x; bicubic 0.00313 s vs 0.07111 s, about 23x; to 5478x3424 Lanczos 0.10035 s vs 1.22571 s, about 12x. Across all 12 scale cases the file gives 11.2x to 22.7x over Wand and 2.9x to 7.8x over Pillow 7.0.0 (all ratios derived from page data), so the README's 'always 16 to 40 times faster than ImageMagick' is not reproduced by this file (the upscale cases fall to 11-12x). Independent: libvips wiki table (crop, 10% bilinear shrink, 3x3 sharpen, save, 10000x10000 TIFF, Threadripper PRO 3955WX, Ubuntu 25.04): pillow-simd 9.5.0 1.51 s vs ImageMagick 7.1.1 convert 4.44 s, about 2.9x (derived from page data); libvips (vips-c 8.18) is faster still at 0.57 s.
corrections.workload: pillow-perf scale suite: resize a 2560x1600 RGB image (synthetic color_circle.png upscaled) to 26x16, 320x200, 2048x1280 and 5478x3424 with bilinear, bicubic and Lanczos filters (ImageMagick via Wand with triangle, catrom and lanczos, MAGICK_THREAD_LIMIT=1); run.py reports the median, of 11 runs for the Pillow-SIMD builds and of 5 runs for Pillow 7.0.0 and Wand (auto/run.sh passes -n5). Independent libvips/vips-bench pipeline: load 10000x10000 TIFF, crop 100 px, shrink 10% bilinear, 3x3 sharpen, save.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: pillow-perf auto/run.sh builds each Pillow-SIMD tag with CFLAGS='-msse4' or '-mavx2' via 'python setup.py develop' with the system cc (ccache cc in the bento/ubuntu-16.04 Vagrant box); the compiler and version are not printed in c5.large.txt. libvips table: Pillow-SIMD installed with pip (vips-bench README); flags not stated.
corrections.hardware: AWS EC2 c5.large (CPU model not printed in the file); libvips table: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX 16-core, Ubuntu 25.04. Other pillow-perf result files cover i5-4430, AMD A10-7800, c3/c4/m5a.large and MacBooks.
corrections.caveats: pillow-perf is maintained by the Pillow-SIMD author, so its numbers are first-party; the README's '16 to 40 times' figure lives on the blocked github.io page, and the checked-in c5.large file shows 11-23x. Different precision: ImageMagick in the pillow-perf run comes from Ubuntu's libmagickwand-dev (ImageMagick 6 Q16, 16-bit quantum) while Pillow-SIMD works in 8-bit fixed point; the Wand path also includes Python binding overhead and an image clone per run. Pillow-SIMD 7.0.0 in the result file is old. In the libvips table pillow-simd is single-threaded while ImageMagick may thread, and the task includes TIFF load and save, not only resampling. Language filter mismatch: Pillow-SIMD is a CPython extension (C kernels with SSE4/AVX2 behind a Python API), not a standalone C/C++ library, so it is not directly callable from C++. ImageMagick (on the category list) is present; stb_image_resize is not. GitHub fork of python-pillow/Pillow that tracks Pillow releases.

notes: All c5.large.txt numbers verified; the record wrongly said 'mean of 11 runs' (it is a median, 5 runs for Wand and Pillow). The libvips wiki row is independent and lifts the tier to B. License is MIT-CMU per the LICENSE file, and the repository is a GitHub fork of python-pillow/Pillow.
